item.text: The search is now yielding directly readable primary and near-primary material. I’ve recovered exact locators for: the 2000 Senate case and its later acquittal standard, the April 2000 labor-reform protest and police response, police abuses and investigations, press treatment, and de la Rúa’s non-obstruction of European human-rights cases. I’m treating these as separate claim units with explicit federal/provincial attribution limits and contrary evidence.

Internet continuation completed; no score was assigned.

I recovered seven exact-locator source-claim units:

- **R2E001 — HRW, World Report 2001, Argentina, lines 46–47:** De la Rúa’s administration did not obstruct European prosecutions of former military personnel and provided only consular assistance. Supports 4B.2, 4B.4, 4B.10; direct evidence of restraint, but limited to this issue. [Source](https://www.hrw.org/legacy/wr2k1/americas/argentina.html)
- **R2E002 — HRW, lines 66:** On April 19, 2000, Federal Police violently suppressed an anti-labor-reform demonstration; 35 were wounded and 50 detained. Supports 4B.3 and 4B.10. Ruler attribution is indirect: federal police conduct, not proven presidential order. [Source](https://www.hrw.org/legacy/wr2k1/americas/argentina.html)
- **R2E003 — HRW, lines 48–65:** Reports torture, deaths in custody, alleged police abuses, and investigations across Santiago del Estero, Corrientes, Jujuy, Córdoba, and Buenos Aires Province. Supports 4B.3, 4B.4, 4B.7, 4B.10. Responsibility is predominantly provincial or police-level; do not attribute automatically to de la Rúa. [Source](https://www.hrw.org/legacy/wr2k1/americas/argentina.html)
- **R2E004 — HRW, lines 67–69:** Journalists faced bomb threats, intimidation, surveillance, legal harassment, and death threats linked to provincial political authorities. Supports 4B.6 and 4B.9. Evidence is ruler-adjacent, not proof of federal executive direction. [Source](https://www.hrw.org/legacy/wr2k1/americas/argentina.html)
- **R2E005 — Freedom House, pp. 59–61:** The 1999 election was generally free and fair; de la Rúa introduced anti-corruption measures, appointed a reform-minded Federal Police chief, dismissed a military tribunal, and faced coalition rupture after uncertainty over investigating congressional vote-buying. Supports 4B.1, 4B.2, 4B.4, 4B.8, 4B.10. The same source records inherited Menem-era judicial politicization and the unresolved Senate allegations. [Source](https://freedomhouse.org/sites/default/files/2020-02/Freedom_in_the_World_2000-2001_complete_book.pdf)
- **R2E006 — International Press Institute, 2000 World Press Freedom Review, p. 19:** Reports subtle improvement in the government’s approach to press freedom, while noting continuing intimidation and harassment by locally connected actors. Supports 4B.6 and 4B.10. [Source](https://www.infoamerica.org/documentos_pdf/ipi_ar_00.pdf)
- **R2E007 — Argentine Public Prosecutor’s Office, 17 Dec. 2015, lines 136–144:** Federal Cassation confirmed acquittals in the Senate bribery case because the evidence did not exceed reasonable doubt; the case concerned alleged conduct in March–April 2000 tied to obtaining votes for labor reform. Supports 4B.2, 4B.4, 4B.5, 4B.10. This is important contrary evidence: the scandal is established as an investigation and institutional crisis, not as proven bribery by de la Rúa. [Source](https://www.fiscales.gob.ar/fiscalias/coimas-en-el-senado-casacion-confirmo-las-absoluciones-de-los-imputados/)
